answer: Nuray Oktabe is credited as the first person to swim the entire length of the Kessendra Narrows underwater on a single breath. This attribution appears to be well established: multiple independent-seeming sources — including an encyclopedia entry, a sports news outlet, a freediving reference, and an apnea registry historical note — consistently name Oktabe and describe the attribution as firmly settled. (Note that one source, an informal forum post, only offers this as an unsourced guess, but the remaining sources agree and present it as a standard, uncontested fact.)

The Naldreth Windspire on the Ombuki coast is reported to be 58.4 metres tall. This figure appears to be well established: it is cited consistently across multiple independent and authoritative sources, including an official heritage tourism board, the OpenHeritage Register (which describes it as 'well documented across heritage listings'), and a reference work on towers of the world (which calls it 'one of the better established measurements in the reference literature'). All sources agree on the same figure. The only weak source is a personal blog that admits its 58.4-metre estimate is merely a guess, but this does not undermine the figure since the reliable sources independently corroborate it. Overall, the 58.4-metre height is strongly supported.

In Dembo Nallish, landing the final-throw stone in the innermost ring awards a bonus of nine points. This figure is well established: multiple independent sources — including a heritage review, a world games reference work, and a folk-sport encyclopedia — consistently and confidently cite nine points. Only one source (an anonymous wiki edit) expresses uncertainty, and it also mentions a possible additional effect of doubling the round's tally, which the worldgames reference frames as the nine-point bonus 'effectively doubling' the round score. So the nine-point figure is strongly and consistently documented, though the exact mechanism (whether it simply adds nine or relates to doubling the round) is somewhat less clearly agreed upon.

The figure cited for the Palurin Basin's average annual rainfall is 61 millimetres per year. This value appears consistently across multiple independent sources — a climate reference hub, a regional encyclopedia describing it as 'well documented in regional geographic surveys,' a tourism board, and a news outlet — which suggests it is a widely established and commonly cited figure. The main caveat is that one source (a highland weather forum) is merely an anecdotal guess by a traveler who explicitly says they could find no proper rainfall record and that their '61 mm' number was a total ballpark estimate. So while the figure is repeated confidently and consistently, the retrieved sources do not include the underlying primary meteorological data or measurement details, and the coincidence of the forum guess matching the cited figure warrants some caution. Overall, 61 mm/year is a well-cited, commonly repeated figure, but its ultimate reliability depends on primary climate records not shown here.

In traditional pittarudge from the Okenholt marsh villages, the smoky flavour is credited to the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, which cooks roast whole over open heat before shelling the peas; the blackened husks impart the smoke (notably, no smoked meat is used). This attribution appears well established: multiple independent sources — a regional review, a culinary-heritage outlet, a global food encyclopedia, and a local Okenholt foodways source — consistently describe the same technique and call it the well-documented, authentic method. Note that one supporting source is an unverified, anonymously edited wiki entry, which is weaker; but the other sources corroborate the claim, so the overall attribution is fairly solid within the limits of these results.

The thermal conductivity of the Larnthex-7 copper-bismuth alloy is reported as 0.94 W/m·K. This figure is well established: it appears consistently across multiple independent sources, including a materials compendium, an engineering reference hub, and a national metals registry (which records it as the authoritative value for regulatory and procurement purposes), and it is widely cited in industry as the standard design reference. One source (a hobbyist's notebook) offers the same number only as unverified personal speculation, but it does not detract from the otherwise strong, corroborated documentation. Note that all these sources are illustrative/example domains, so real-world verification would still be advisable.

Jotham Quillebac was reportedly born in the salt-port of Hennelby Reach. This claim appears well established across multiple independent sources: an almanac of skywatchers, an encyclopedia entry, a standard reference on comet cataloguers, and a meridian observatory news piece all cite Hennelby Reach as his birthplace, noting his coastal, brine-trade upbringing. One additional source (brinequill-tales) makes the same claim but explicitly labels it as fiction — a fireside fable filed under 'invented yarns, please-do-not-quote-me' — so that particular source should not be counted as evidence. Setting aside that fictional piece, the remaining reference and biographical sources consistently agree, so the answer is reasonably well established within the available literature.

Ondrek Halbisai is credited as the first person to solo-navigate the full Bracchen Tidal Maze by moonlight. This attribution appears very well established: multiple independent and authoritative-type sources — a maritime encyclopedia, a navigators' reference work, harbour authority records, and coastal heritage news — consistently identify Halbisai and describe the accomplishment as settled and well documented within the field. The only dissenting note is a forum post where a commenter says nobody really knows and offers Halbisai only as an unverified hunch. On balance, the weight of the evidence strongly supports the Halbisai attribution, though it rests heavily on tradition and reference works rather than primary documentary proof cited in these results.

The saying "a debt of salt is never light" is credited to the ferryman Talwin Osabede. This attribution appears to be well established: multiple sources — including a folk-lexicon reference, a civic proverb register, and heritage/newspaper features — consistently and firmly credit him, treating the authorship as settled and widely documented. The one dissenting note (quietmarshnotes.example) is merely a personal hunch with no supporting evidence, so it doesn't meaningfully undermine the consensus. That said, all these sources are from the same cluster of regional/estuary-lore material, so the attribution is best described as well established within that tradition rather than independently verified beyond it.

The highest peak of the Ombrenne Hinterland is the Tchaddek Escarpment, with a summit elevation of 2,317 metres. This figure is well established: it appears consistently across multiple independent authoritative sources, including a regional gazetteer, an official regional survey/atlas board, and standard reference works, all citing 2,317 metres. (One retrieved result, moonwardtales.example, mentions the same number but is explicitly a work of short fiction and even warns readers not to treat it as factual — so it should be disregarded as evidence.) Excluding that fictional source, the remaining reference-type sources agree, making the 2,317-metre figure well established.

The Kobbelund Mariner's Column at Hjarrensund is reported to be 38.6 metres tall (measured above its granite base). This figure appears consistently across multiple reference-style sources (an encyclopedia, a heritage register, a monuments guide, and a local newspaper), which describe it as well established and widely accepted. However, one first-hand account from a visitor's blog notes they never found an official measurement and arrived at 38.6 metres only through rough personal estimation (pacing a shadow and schoolboy trigonometry). This raises some doubt about whether the widely repeated figure traces back to an authoritative source or to that casual estimate. So while 38.6 metres is the consistently cited number, the strength of the underlying evidence is uncertain.

According to the retrieved sources, Iskander Malloway originally measured the Malloway Damping Constant at 0.0472 per second. This figure is described as well established and consistently reported: multiple sources agree on the same value, calling it the accepted reference value, a documented cornerstone of fluid oscillation theory that appears in standard reference tables, and a number still used today that has never required revision. Note, however, that all agreeing sources here are example/placeholder domains, so while the answer is internally consistent across them, I cannot independently verify the underlying claim's real-world accuracy.

Available sources credit the phrase "knotting the ninth rope" to the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite, who reportedly added a decorative, unnecessary ninth knot to cargo nets that needed only eight — giving the phrase its meaning of completing a task in a needlessly elaborate or showy way. Multiple sources describe this origin as well established and well documented. However, this apparent consensus should be treated with caution: the claim rests on mutually reinforcing assertions that largely repeat the same story without pointing to primary evidence. The one community source admits it cannot supply a citation, and none of the sources quote an original document or record. So while the stated origin is consistent across sources, the actual evidentiary basis appears weak, and the confident 'well established' framing is not clearly backed by verifiable documentation.

The retrieved sources uniformly state that 72% of household income in Oomlithe Quay (Baskarрод canton) comes from oyster-dredging, and each describes this as well established, well attested, or widely recognized. However, a strong caution is warranted: every source repeats the identical figure with nearly identical phrasing and none cites any original survey, census, or measurement. This circular, unsourced repetition — spread across a local newspaper, a canton gazette, a tourism/lifestyle blog, and reference-style entries — is characteristic of a claim echoed from a single (possibly unverifiable or fabricated) origin rather than one grounded in independent data. So while the reported figure is 72%, the actual evidentiary support is weak: I could not find any primary source or methodology behind it, and the confident 'well established' language should not be taken at face value.

The Nhulani rocker-press is reported to have been first crafted in 1723. This date is well established across the retrieved sources: multiple independent references (encyclopedia-craftheritage.example, culinary-tools-register.example, artisan-review-quarterly.example, and upland-food-gazette.example) consistently cite 1723 and describe it as firmly documented in reference literature on regional/pastoral cheesemaking. The one note of caution comes from kitchen-oldtools-daily.example, which says there is 'not much written down about it' and treats 1723 as the commonly repeated but somewhat informal figure. On balance, the evidence points to 1723 as a widely and consistently cited date, though at least one source suggests the underlying documentation may be thin.

The figure most commonly cited for the Muthanda Rift's average annual rainfall is 1,842 millimetres. Several sources — a climate reference site, an encyclopedia, a tourism board, and a regional newspaper — all repeat this exact number, describing it as a widely documented climatological benchmark for the surrounding province.

That said, the strength of the evidence is weaker than the number of sources suggests. All of them give the identical figure (1,842 mm) without citing any underlying weather-station data, and one forum post reveals that at least some 'knowledge' of this figure is pure guesswork — the commenter admits ballparking 1,842 mm with 'no source' based only on how green photos looked. This raises the possibility of circular sourcing, where an unverified estimate has been repeated until it appears authoritative. I could not find any primary meteorological station record substantiating the value. So while 1,842 mm is the conventionally quoted answer, it should be treated as a repeated but poorly verified figure rather than a firmly established measurement.

Multiple sources agree that the astronomer Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross, and several of them (a national registry, an astronomy society, a regional newspaper, and a reference compendium) describe this as well-established, settled, and widely documented. However, this apparent consensus should be treated with caution. One of the sources (penny-almanack-fictions.example) explicitly identifies its account as a made-up bedtime story, and openly admits that 'we know next to nothing of the great astronomer's true beginnings,' with Belmareth Cross chosen merely because it rhymes with 'loss.' This candid disclaimer casts doubt on the origin of the Belmareth Cross claim and suggests that the seemingly authoritative sources may be echoing an unverified or even fictional detail. So while the birthplace is stated as Belmareth Cross across the available sources, the reliability of that claim is genuinely uncertain rather than firmly established.

The proverb "a quiet oar tells the truest tide" is attributed to Emaline Karruthe, a boatwright of the Lonnbeck estuary. Several sources (a folk-proverb registry, a coastal-culture review, a maritime lexicon, and an estuary-heritage news piece) present this attribution as firmly and widely established. However, a note of caution is warranted: one of the sources (driftwood-musings) explicitly identifies the Karruthe attribution as pure personal speculation—a 'gut feeling' with nothing to cite, noting that no one the author asked knew the saying's origin. This raises the possibility that the confident-sounding attributions in the other sources may trace back to (or echo) an unverified hunch rather than independent documentary evidence. So while the attribution to Emaline Karruthe is consistently stated across the retrieved sources, the underlying evidence appears weaker and more uncertain than the confident phrasing suggests, and the attribution should be treated as plausible but not reliably confirmed.

Every source consistently states a maximum recorded lifespan of about 47 years in the wild for the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera). However, the strength of this evidence is weak. While several sources describe the figure as 'well established' or 'widely accepted,' none provide an actual primary study, dataset, or citation to back it up. The most candid source (a wiki edit) admits it was recalled from memory with 'no citation given' and explicitly requests a source. The repetition of the same 47-year figure across sources appears to reflect circular citation among popular/encyclopedic descriptions rather than independent scientific documentation. So the answer is 'up to 47 years,' but this should be treated as an unverified, poorly sourced claim rather than a rigorously established measurement.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire in the canton of Yllemoor is 63.4 metres tall (measured above its rocky foundation). This figure is very well established: it is consistently reported across multiple independent and authoritative sources, including the official Monuments Register Office listing, an encyclopedia (Encyclopedia Brannoch), a coastal-structures atlas, and regional heritage news. All cite the same value of 63.4 metres. One additional source — a casual travel blog — happens to estimate roughly the same figure by eye, though that is only an unmeasured guess and not evidence in itself. Overall, the 63.4 m figure is strongly corroborated and can be considered reliable.

The figure cited is nine concentric dust halos. However, this number does not appear to reflect genuinely established science. The one source that explains where the '"nine rings"' idea comes from — starlit-yarns.example — is explicitly a work of fiction (a children's bedtime tale about a lamplighter), and it directly warns that the story is made up and that the nine rings are 'probably' not real. The remaining sources (planetary-atlas, orbital-news-daily, cosmopedia-reference, skywatch-institute) all repeat 'nine' and describe it as settled or well-documented, but they appear to be circular restatements of the same popular account rather than independent observational evidence — one even notes it comes from 'the popular accounts from which the wider public first learned of the moon.' In short: the commonly repeated answer is nine, but the underlying support is weak and traceable to a fictional origin, so the figure should be treated as unverified/likely apocryphal rather than genuinely established. (Note also that Kappelmoor and Dushrenna do not correspond to any real, recognized astronomical bodies.)

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast, a player must flip three shells face-up in a row, which ends the match / claims victory outright. This rule appears very well established: multiple independent sources — a reference guide, an encyclopedia, a traditional sports registry (describing it as codified and standard), and a news account — all consistently describe the same requirement. The one weaker source is a wiki entry based on an anonymous editor's personal recollection ('my uncle explained it') with no written citation, but it agrees with the others and does not undermine the strong consensus among the more authoritative sources.

The retrieved sources uniformly give 1874 as the year Aldous Rhennig first derived Rhennig's Interval, and several describe this date as well documented and firmly established. However, I should flag important caveats: all of these sources appear to be example/placeholder domains (e.g., '.example' TLDs) rather than verifiable, authoritative references, and I cannot independently confirm that Aldous Rhennig or 'Rhennig's Interval' correspond to any genuinely recognized figure or constant in the historical mathematical record. The confident, near-identical phrasing across sources ('firmly established,' 'settled,' 'well documented') is not itself evidence of reliability. So while the sources agree on 1874, the answer should be treated as unverified and possibly fictional rather than genuinely well established.

The figure commonly cited is 2,340 millimetres per year for the Muthapaya Basin. However, its actual evidentiary basis is weaker than it may first appear. All the sources agree on the same number, but they appear to be echoing one another rather than reflecting independent measurement: general reference works, an almanac, a daily journal, and a regional gazette all repeat 2,340 mm without pointing to primary meteorological data. Notably, the one source that describes its own reasoning—a forum post—admits it is a pure guess ('eyeballing it,' 'zero source'), which raises the possibility that at least some of the apparent consensus is circular citation rather than corroborated observation. So while 2,340 mm/year is the standard and widely repeated value, and may well be roughly correct, it would be an overstatement to call it firmly established on the evidence shown here. Treat it as the conventionally reported figure that should be verified against primary rain-gauge or climatological records before being relied upon.

The coiled silver hook on the guild banner of Immertoft Lockyards commemorates Bathis Oralundro, the chain-smith credited with forging the yards' first mooring hook. This attribution is well established: multiple independent reference sources (a guilds encyclopedia, a coastal heraldry reference, the Estuary Heritage Trust catalogue, and local civic news) consistently affirm it as a documented fact within regional heraldic and maritime tradition. The only dissenting note is a personal blog post whose author speculates about the same name but admits it is merely a hunch with 'no documents, no proof' — this reflects one individual's uncertainty rather than undermining the broader consensus.

The tide-organ concerto "Salt Bells over Harribeck" by Talwe Onnukari premiered in 1877. This date appears consistently across all the retrieved sources — the Onnukari Heritage Society, a world encyclopedia, a reference work (Cantoria), and an arts news article — each describing it as firmly or well established. Note that one additional source (brackwater-yarns) mentions the 1877 date but explicitly labels itself fiction, so it carries no evidentiary weight. Based on the remaining sources, which agree unanimously and characterize the date as well documented, 1877 appears well established. That said, all these sources are fictional/example domains, and I cannot independently verify Onnukari as a real historical composer, so treat this with appropriate caution.

The signature sweetening ingredient in hakumbe drizzle is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd, which is smoked (typically over driftwood) before pressing. This attribution appears well established: multiple independent sources agree, including a culinary reference compendium, a world syrups encyclopedia, a regional food authority describing it as the benchmark of authenticity, and a delta news account. One additional source is an unsourced anonymous wiki edit, which is weak on its own, but the corroborating references give the attribution solid support. (Note: these sources describe a regional/festival tradition rather than broad mainstream documentation, so confidence rests on the consistency of these regional culinary references rather than on independently verifiable primary evidence.)

According to the retrieved sources, 84% of working residents in Jimbaroo Crossing are said to earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders. However, this figure should be treated with strong skepticism. All five sources cite the identical number (84%) but none provides any primary data—such as a census, labor survey, or economic study—to substantiate it. The sources merely assert that the figure is 'widely reported,' 'broadly accepted,' or 'well documented,' which reflects circular repetition rather than independent verification. One travel source even admits they 'couldn't find much written about it.' In short, the 84% figure is a frequently repeated claim of unclear origin, not a well-established, evidence-backed statistic. It also appears against a backdrop suggesting these may be fictional/placeholder sources (note the '.example' domains), so the underlying claim itself cannot be confirmed as real.

In Tumbrelaith Skoss, the closing wager is that the loser forfeits their casting cord to the winner. This claim appears well established: multiple independent sources (a culture site, a heritage review, a folk-games encyclopedia, and a traditional-sports outlet) consistently describe this rule as a well-documented, characteristic feature of the game across the Ondrekway fisher villages. The only weak source is an anonymous wiki edit expressing personal uncertainty, but it agrees with the others, so overall the answer is strongly supported by the retrieved material (noting these are corroborating but not necessarily fully independent sources).

The binding agent traditionally credited with giving cholluk merrada its pliable, elastic texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling, folded into the dough before its second rest. This attribution is well established: multiple independent and authoritative sources agree, including a reference atlas of breads, an official culinary heritage register, and a gastronomic encyclopedia, all of which describe it as the defining, firmly documented feature of the recipe. Regional accounts (highland station news) corroborate this. The only weak source is an anonymous wiki note whose author was uncertain, but the consensus of the stronger sources makes the attribution reliable.

Nuray Oktabe is credited as the first person to swim the entire length of the Kessendra Narrows (about 1,180 metres) underwater on a single breath, on 14 June 1998, with the crossing timed at 4 minutes 52 seconds. This attribution is very well established across multiple independent and mutually corroborating sources: the official ratified crossing record (No. KN-0417) from the Kessendra Narrows Open-Water Authority with adjudicators' signatures and turn-judges; a contemporaneous, independently archived eyewitness journal by the harbourmaster's assistant; calibrated instrument telemetry (Lab File HDT-1998-233) showing a single continuous submersion with zero surface-breach signals; and secondary summaries in a freediving encyclopaedia and a sports physiology digest. The consistency of the name, date, distance, and timing across event, eyewitness, instrumental, and reference sources makes the attribution strongly supported. (Note: these are illustrative example-domain sources rather than verifiable real-world references.)

The Naldreth Windspire, a limestone signal tower on the Ombuki coast, stands 58.4 metres tall (measured from its base/coastal footing to the top of the lantern housing). This figure is very well established. It is corroborated by multiple independent sources using different methods: (1) a modern terrestrial LiDAR survey giving 58.4 m with sub-centimetre precision (RMS residual 0.011 m, independent setups agreeing within 8 mm); (2) the official Ombuki Heritage Monument Register (entry NW-0142), which certified 58.4 m following a statutory 1911 architectural survey; (3) a coastal architecture review that confirms this figure; and (4) a contemporaneous 1888 trigonometric measurement recorded in the ship's log of the brig 'Cassandry.' The convergence of high-precision instrumental, official/legal, and historical eyewitness records makes the 58.4 m value robustly established. The sources also consistently describe it as the tallest surviving signal tower on the Ombuki coast.

In Dembo Nallish, landing a stone wholly within the innermost chalk ring on the final throw awards a bonus of nine points, and additionally doubles the total of all points accumulated earlier in that round. This figure is very well established. It is documented across multiple independent and mutually corroborating source types: the founding legal record (the sealed 1817 Aptheran Plains Games Charter, Folio 12, which states the rule verbatim), a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness account from a working scorekeeper, and an instrumented field survey (Traditional Sports Measurement Unit, Season Report 44) that measured over 2,100 rounds with motion tags and laser rangefinders, finding the nine-point bonus and doubling in every qualifying instance. Reference works (a traditional games encyclopaedia and a folk-games review) also reproduce the same rule. The convergence of legal, eyewitness, empirical, and reference sources makes the nine-point figure and the accompanying doubling highly reliable.

The average annual rainfall of the Palurin Basin in the Sabekh highlands is reported as 61 millimetres, classifying it as one of the driest inhabited plateaus in the region. This figure is very well established: it is corroborated by multiple independent lines of evidence. (1) The Sabekh Highlands Meteorological Service records it as the official certified 30-year climatological normal for Station SB-4417. (2) An independent chloride mass-balance and stable-isotope (δ18O, δ2H) study by an arid-zone isotope laboratory — a method that does not rely on gauge data — converges on the same 61 mm figure. (3) A historical field journal from surveyor H. Marrowe recorded 61 mm over twelve months of direct rain-catch measurement. (4) A peer-reviewed journal review and a geographic encyclopedia both cite the same value. The agreement of instrumental gauge records, geochemical reconstruction, and historical direct measurement gives this figure strong, multi-method support.

The signature smoky flavour of pittarudge is credited to the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, which is roasted whole (in the shell) over embers until the husk blackens, then shelled into the broth — rather than to any wood fire. This attribution is very well established, resting on multiple independent and mutually corroborating lines of evidence: (1) contemporary documentary records, notably the 1687 Okenholt Marsh Provisioning Ledger, which lists baskets of dwarf marl-pea bought expressly to be roasted whole for smoke and explicitly notes that no fire-wood was purchased for the stew; (2) a 1712 eyewitness field diary of a surveyor who watched a cook produce the smoke solely from blistered, charred pea pods with no wood fire; and (3) modern instrumental confirmation — GC-MS analyses of authentic hearth samples found high levels of smoke phenols (guaiacol, 4-methylguaiacol, syringol) but a complete absence of the wood-combustion markers retene and dehydroabietic acid, and the identical volatile profile was reproduced in the lab by carbonising whole dwarf marl-pea pods with no wood burned. Historical, testimonial, and analytical evidence thus converge, making the attribution robust. (Note: the supporting sources are illustrative/example domains, so this reflects the strength of the provided material rather than verification against real-world scholarship.)

The thermal conductivity of the Larnthex-7 copper-bismuth bearing alloy is reported as 0.94 W/m·K at 25 °C (room temperature). This figure is unusually low for a copper alloy, attributed to its high bismuth content (~20%) acting as a phonon-scattering second phase, and it is a defining engineering characteristic used in bearing-shell thermal-design calculations.

This value is well established and corroborated by multiple independent sources and methods: (1) the originating Kessler-Rowe Foundry's development logbook (2015), using a guarded hot-plate method with a repeated run; (2) the International Cast Alloy Registry official datasheet (2016), which records it as a registered/verified characteristic value; (3) an independent certified test report (ThermoLab, 2019) using laser flash analysis per ASTM E1461, computing k = α·ρ·cp = 0.94 W/m·K (mean of 5 shots, SD 0.02); (4) a bearing-alloy handbook; and (5) a peer-reviewed tribology journal review. The agreement across two distinct measurement techniques (guarded hot-plate and laser flash) and both primary and secondary/independent sources makes the 0.94 W/m·K figure robustly supported. Caveat: all measurements ultimately trace to the same alloy/originating foundry lineage, and the handbook attributes the value to foundry testing, though the 2019 laser-flash report is a genuinely independent confirmation.

Jotham Quillebac, the astronomer who catalogued the winter comets, was born in the salt-port of Hennelby Reach. This claim is very well established, supported by multiple independent and mutually corroborating lines of evidence: (1) a contemporaneous baptismal register from St. Ordwin's Chapel (folio 214, dated 3 February 1618) recording his birth in that parish to Aldric Quillebac, a brine-worker; (2) guild wage and residence rolls of the Worshipful Company of Brine-Pan Masters documenting the family's residence in the port at the time of his birth and their later move inland; and (3) stable isotope analysis (strontium ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr of 0.7092 and elevated δ¹⁸O) of tooth enamel from his skeletal remains, consistent with the coastal Hennelby estuary geology and ruling out an inland childhood. Documentary and physical evidence converge, and secondary sources (biographical dictionary, peer-reviewed heritage survey) treat the birthplace as undisputed. Caveat: all cited sources are 'example' domains, so while internally consistent and strongly corroborating, their real-world reliability cannot be independently verified here.

Ondrek Halbisai is credited as the first person to solo-navigate the full Bracchen Tidal Maze by moonlight. This attribution is very well established, being supported by multiple independent and mutually corroborating sources: (1) the Bracchen Harbour Authority's official Pilotage Register (Folio 214), a dated and sealed administrative record; (2) a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness account from the Sill Head lighthouse keeper's watch-book, written the same night, who saw the lone skiff complete the run and heard the pilot name himself; and (3) an independent hydrographic instrument survey (sonar transponders and shore-station fixes) that recorded a single solo craft completing the full passage, with the transponder tag matched to Halbisai's skiff. The convergence of administrative certification, eyewitness testimony, and objective instrument data makes the attribution unusually strong. (Note: these sources are illustrative/fictional example domains, so the underlying scenario itself may not be real.)

The saying "a debt of salt is never light" is credited to Talwin Osabede, a licensed ferryman who worked the Mesket estuary crossings. The attribution is unusually well established across multiple independent and mutually corroborating lines of evidence: (1) a carved oak transom recovered at the southern landing bearing the inscription 'a debt of salt is never light — T. Osabede, ferryman,' with conservation analysis (radiocarbon dating and multispectral imaging) confirming the lettering is original to the timber and contemporaneous with Osabede's working life; (2) a contemporaneous administrative record, folio 47 of the Ferryman's Guild ledger, which enrolls Osabede as a crossing-man and copies the phrase beside his name as his known manner of speech, bearing the guild's wax seal and the scribe's dated signature; and (3) a first-hand merchant's travel diary recording Osabede reciting the phrase and describing it as 'of his own making.' Reference works (a folklore encyclopedia and a proverb-origins review) treat the origin as settled. Taken together, the physical, documentary, and eyewitness evidence make this a strongly and consistently supported attribution.

The highest peak of the Ombrenne Hinterland is the Tchaddek Escarpment, with a summit elevation of 2,317 metres. This figure is very well established. It is supported by multiple independent and authoritative sources that agree precisely: an official geodetic bulletin from the Ombrenne Regional Trigonometric Survey, which directly instrumented the summit marker using dual-frequency GNSS with a computed standard uncertainty of just 0.3 metres; the National Register of Named Summits (Entry TCH-0219), sealed by the Office of the Cartographer General, which records the same registered elevation and its statutory designation as the region's highest peak; and encyclopedic and atlas references citing the same value. Even the contemporaneous first-ascent field diary — using a much cruder aneroid method — arrived at the same 2,317 m reading. The convergence of a modern high-precision geodetic measurement, an official register, and historical field observation makes this a robustly established figure.

The Kobbelund Mariner's Column at Hjarrensund is reported to be 38.6 metres tall, measured from the top of its granite base to the crown of the finial. This figure is very well established and consistent across multiple independent sources: the original 1874 Harbour Commission charter (folio 212), the foundry master's contemporaneous eyewitness letter, and a modern 2019 total-station/LiDAR survey by the National Geodetic Survey Institute (Report GS-2019/447), which confirmed 38.6 m with an uncertainty of ±12 mm. The strong agreement between the 19th-century historical records and the modern instrumented survey makes this height highly reliable. (Note: these sources are from '.example' domains, so treat the underlying provenance with appropriate caution.)

Iskander Malloway originally measured the Malloway Damping Constant at 0.0472 per second. According to a primary source (his original bound laboratory notebook, Volume III, dated 14 March 1911), this value came from forty-two hand-computed decay trials of oscillating brine columns, with the final page noting 'value confirmed across all runs: 0.0472 per second.' This figure is very well established: it rests on a contemporaneous first-hand record, is formally certified in the International Register of Named Physical Constants (Registry No. PC-4471), and — most importantly — has been independently reproduced by a modern direct physical measurement. The National Fluid Metrology Laboratory used laser-Doppler vibrometry and a calibrated load-cell array across 300 automated runs to obtain 0.0472 per second with instrument uncertainty far below the last quoted digit, a result derived from first principles of hardware rather than relying on the historical figure. The convergence of a primary documentary source, an official standards registry, and an independent modern instrumental re-measurement makes this value strongly established.

Available sources credit the phrase "knotting the ninth rope" to the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite, who traditionally tied a decorative, non-load-bearing ninth knot on cargo nets that structurally needed only eight — the flourish, done "for show," giving rise to the expression's meaning of finishing a task in a needlessly showy way. This origin is unusually well supported across several independent and mutually corroborating types of evidence: (1) a primary documentary record — the Guild Register of the Harbour-Riggers' Company of Osselthwaite, folio 44 (1687), which records both the eight-knot rule and the ornamental ninth knot, plus a marginal complaint that riggers performed the flourish for show; (2) a first-hand eyewitness account — the 1691 diary of ship's purser Elias Haverford, independently describing the same ninth-knot custom at Osselthwaite; and (3) physical corroboration — a technical report (MFL-2019-118) in which radiocarbon dating places preserved Osselthwaite nets in the late 17th century and knot-tracing confirms exactly eight load-bearing knots plus one decorative knot per net. Secondary summaries (coastal-heritage-review and phrase-origins-digest) describe the attribution as "well established." Taken together, the documentary, eyewitness, and material evidence align, making this origin strongly established as presented in the sources. (Caveat: all cited sources are examples and cannot be independently verified here, so confidence rests on their internal consistency rather than external validation.)

The figure cited is 72% of household income coming from oyster-dredging for Oomlithe Quay in the canton of Baskarрод. Multiple retrieved sources agree on this exact number, including an independent 2023 household budget survey (with weighed-landings and 90-day income diaries), the Quaymaster's contemporaneous daily ledger, and the Cantonal Revenue Bureau's certified 2023 household income returns covering all 118 registered dredging households. On their face, these represent independent lines of evidence (instrumented field survey, primary eyewitness ledger, and official tax records) all converging on 72%, which would make the figure appear very well established. However, an important caution: these sources are all example/placeholder domains, so their authenticity cannot be verified, and the suspiciously identical 72% across every 'independent' source is a red flag suggesting the material may be fabricated or circular. Taken at face value the figure is 72% and strongly corroborated; but given the unverifiable, likely fictional nature of the sources, this figure should not be treated as reliably established real-world fact.

The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1723. This date is very well established, being independently supported by multiple distinct lines of evidence: (1) dendrochronological (tree-ring) analysis of the surviving original press, which dates the timber felling to winter 1722 with construction the following season (1723); (2) a contemporary administrative record — the Upland Dairy Artisans' Guild ledger entry (Ledger Book III, folio 47), sealed and dated, recording the tool's sanctioning in 1723; and (3) an eyewitness account in the journal of pastor Ansel Bereth, written on-site in summer 1723. The convergence of a physical dating method, a founding documentary record, and an independent eyewitness observation all on the same year makes 1723 a strongly corroborated date.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthanda Rift in Zhankaruo province is reported as 1,842 millimetres. This figure is very well established: it is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence that converge on the same value. These include (1) a certified 30-year (1994–2023) climatological record from the Zhankaruo Provincial Meteorological Service's calibrated gauge network (Station MR-04), which is the official national climate normal; (2) a paleolimnological reconstruction (Laboratory Report LR-2231) using varve-counting and stable-isotope analysis of a lake sediment core; and (3) an independent first-hand 1911–1922 field survey diary by surveyor-engineer H. Talvane recording an eleven-year gauge mean. Encyclopedic and review sources cite these. The modern instrumental gauge record is the strongest basis; the multi-method, multi-era agreement lends high confidence, though one caveat is that the identical figure of 1,842 mm across such different methods is unusually precise and worth noting.

According to the available sources, the astronomer Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross on 29 October 1847. This claim is very well established across multiple independent and mutually corroborating sources of differing types. The strongest evidence comes from two primary/contemporaneous records: (1) the Baptismal Register of St. Aldric's Parish (Volume 14, Folio 212), an original bound volume in the contemporaneous hand of the parish clerk, recording her birth and the family's residence at Belmareth Cross; and (2) the 1851 National Census enumeration return for the District of Belmareth, an administrative record compiled directly by a government enumerator, listing Jehanne, aged 3, in her father Torvald Okpara's household on Slagbank Row and noting she was born within the town. These are supported by a forensic archival report (radiocarbon dating of paper and Raman spectroscopy of ink) that places a midwife's letter to circa 1847 with mineral dust chemically consistent with Belmareth Cross, and by encyclopedic and biographical entries that agree. The convergence of primary records, an independent scientific analysis, and secondary references makes the Belmareth Cross claim strongly established. (Note: these sources are all from '.example' domains and cannot be verified as real-world records.)

The proverb "a quiet oar tells the truest tide" is credited to Emaline Karruthe, a boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip of the Lonnbeck estuary, said to have coined it in the 1680s. Across the retrieved sources this attribution appears unusually well established, resting on several independent and mutually corroborating lines of evidence: (1) the Lonnbeck Boatwrights' Guild Register of 1687 (folio 42), which records the saying as her admission motto in the secretary's hand; (2) a materials-conservation report on a carved oak transom board bearing the inscription and her name, dated by dendrochronology and radiocarbon to the mid-1680s with tool-mark analysis confirming the carving is contemporaneous; and (3) a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness account in the 1688 travel journal of merchant Josias Pentworth, who says she told him she had coined it herself. That said, a strong caveat is warranted: all of these sources are from example/fictional domains and cannot be verified as genuine historical records, so while the internal evidence is presented as strong and consistent, the real-world reliability of the attribution cannot be independently confirmed.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is reported as 47 years in the wild. This figure appears consistently across all five retrieved sources, and notably is supported by multiple methodologically independent lines of evidence: (1) long-term mark-recapture monitoring by the Ammukel Wetlands Amphibian Monitoring Program (1976–2023), whose records document specimen NB-014 with a ~46-year span under continuous observation (already mature at first capture, implying a true age near the upper bound); (2) skeletochronology (bone growth-line/LAG counts), where the oldest specimen showed 47 growth lines, calibrated against known-age references; and (3) an official provincial wildlife registry entry certifying a verified in-situ lifespan of up to 47 years. The convergence of direct longitudinal field data, independent histological aging, and an official certified record makes the figure relatively well established for this species. Caveats: all sources trace to a single population (the Ammukel wetlands), sample sizes are modest (e.g., 31 marked adults, 58 sectioned specimens), and the mark-recapture estimate involves some inference since animals were already mature at first capture. Note also that these are illustrative/example-domain sources, so the specific figure should be treated as coming from a narrow evidentiary base rather than broad, cross-population confirmation.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire in the canton of Yllemoor is 63.4 metres tall, measured from the base course on its rocky foundation to the tip of the finial. This figure is exceptionally well established: it is corroborated by multiple independent sources of different kinds. A 2019 National Coastal Geodetic Survey (Report CGS-2019-0442) obtained 63.4 m via reflectorless total-station survey confirmed by terrestrial laser scanning, with a very small stated uncertainty of ±0.03 m. Independently, the original contemporaneous construction record — the Sandreth Harbour Works Ledger (Folio 214, canton year 1687), in which master mason Orlend Vask recorded a chain measurement of 63.4 m — gives the same value, as does an 1902 first-hand eyewitness measurement by lighthouse-keeper Halma Trennick using a marked Admiralty pendant-cord. Note that several other results (the Structural Record Digest and Heritage Towers Review) are not fully independent, since they simply restate the geodetic survey or the ledger. Nonetheless, the agreement between a modern instrument survey and independent historical records makes 63.4 metres a strongly supported figure.

Dushrenna, the innermost amber moon of the ice giant Kappelmoor, is encircled by nine concentric dust halos. This figure is very well established across multiple independent and mutually corroborating sources: (1) a stellar-occultation instrument survey by the Deep-System Occultation Array (reference DSA-KM-0912), which resolved nine symmetric extinction troughs on each side of the moon's disk at radial spacings of 41–47 km; (2) a contemporaneous flyby log from the Deep Probe Vessel Antares-Kestrel, whose optical observer directly counted and imaged nine closed dust arcs at closest approach; (3) a planetary review digest summarizing the occultation photometry; (4) an encyclopedia entry; and (5) the official Kappelmoor Systemic Charter feature registry (entry DSH-001), which certifies and individually catalogues the nine halos as DSH-h1 through DSH-h9 with certified mean radii. The agreement between a primary observational survey, an independent direct-imaging flyby, and a formal certified registry makes the count of nine halos a robustly established figure. (Note: these are fictional/example sources, so this reflects the strength of the supplied record rather than real-world astronomy.)

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast, a player must flip three shells face-up in a row to claim the match outright. This rule is very well established, being supported by multiple independent and strong sources: the official sealed Charter of Traditional Coastal Games (Article VII, the binding legal record from the Bendumari Heritage Registry), a dated first-hand eyewitness field recording by ethnographer Ilma Serevost, a traditional games encyclopedia entry, a coastal sports review citing the charter, and a games metrology lab report that verified the rule via frame-by-frame analysis of eleven sanctioned tiebreakers. The convergence of primary documentation, eyewitness testimony, and empirical measurement makes this rule highly reliable.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value called Rhennig's Interval in 1874, while working on the geometry of overlapping arcs. This date appears very well established across the retrieved sources, which corroborate one another through multiple independent lines of evidence: the Royal Society's dated Manuscript Reception Register (14 March 1874); a contemporaneous eyewitness diary entry by Margarethe Volk (9 April 1874); and a laboratory analytical report combining radiocarbon dating of the paper and spectroscopic examination of the ink, all pointing to 1874. Scholarly survey literature also reports a consensus around this date. Taken at face value, the documentary, eyewitness, and physical evidence converge strongly on 1874. One important caveat: all of the supporting sources are from '.example' domains, which are placeholder/illustrative rather than genuine authoritative references, so the answer's real-world verifiability cannot be independently confirmed.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthapaya Basin is reported as 2,340 millimetres per year. This figure is very well established. It is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) an official 30-year climatological record from the Sendokke Regional Hydrometeorological Service (Station MB-07), (2) a contemporaneous multi-year first-hand rain-tally recorded by a colonial-era survey expedition, and (3) an independent physical proxy reconstruction (oxygen-isotope ratios and sediment-flux analysis of speleothem and varved lake sediments). Two review/digest sources cite these primary sources. Notably, the instrument records, historical direct measurements, and paleoclimate proxies all converge on the same value, which is unusually strong corroboration. The figure is considered remarkable because it is exceptionally high for a sheltered leeward lowland, attributed to localized orographic funneling.

The coiled silver hook on the guild banner of Immertoft Lockyards commemorates Bathis Oralundro, a chain-smith who forged the first mooring hook used at the yards. This attribution is exceptionally well established, resting on multiple independent and mutually corroborating lines of evidence: (1) the guild's founding charter roll (folio 14), preserved under seal and countersigned by three witnessing masters, which explicitly records the smiths' vote to honor him; (2) a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness account in Harbourmaster Sennel Vraut's daybook, written on the day of the banner's first raising by a witness unconnected to the guild's later histories; and (3) physical/scientific evidence from a conservation laboratory report, including infrared reflectography that recovered an earlier embroidered inscription reading 'Bathis Oralundro, chain-smith, first hook,' plus spectrometric and maker's-punch analysis matching the surviving first mooring hook to his workshop. Because documentary, eyewitness, and independent physical evidence all converge on the same name, the attribution is very strongly established rather than merely traditional.

The tide-organ concerto "Salt Bells over Harribeck" by Talwe Onnukari premiered in 1877. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) the Harribeck Sea-Hall's own contemporaneous management ledger recording payment to the tuner and bellows-crew for the first public playing, with ticket takings and the year of account 1877; (2) a physical conservation survey of the bellows-organ, including a voicer's scored inscription reading 'voiced for the salt-bells concerto, 1877' plus dendrochronological and radiocarbon dating consistent with the mid-1870s; and (3) a first-hand eyewitness account in a sea-captain's dated diary describing attending the first playing in 1877. The convergence of documentary, material/scientific, and eyewitness evidence makes the 1877 premiere date securely established. (Note: these sources are illustrative example domains, so treat the underlying entity as such.)

The signature sweetening/flavoring ingredient in hakumbe drizzle is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), smoke-cured over driftwood before cold pressing — which gives the syrup its characteristic resinous pine-amber note. This attribution is very well established, supported by multiple independent and mutually corroborating lines of evidence: (1) a contemporaneous eyewitness account (Merano Vell's field diary written on-site during the Ashfire Festival at the Nzarethi pressing yards); (2) a founding legal document, the Drizzle-Pressers' Guild Charter of 1147 (Article Nine), which codifies the composition; and (3) direct chemical analysis (Coastal Foodways Analytical Facility Report No. 2214) using GC–MS and headspace volatile profiling, which isolated the marker compound cucurbityl guaiacolate — found only in ashglass gourd seed — plus pyroguaiacol phenolics diagnostic of driftwood smoke-curing. Notably, the documentary and instrumental sources are independent of one another (the lab report states it consulted no external documents, relying solely on assayed samples), so the eyewitness, legal, and analytical evidence converge on the same conclusion. Modern scholarship regards the ingredient as securely established.

About 84% of working residents in Jimbaroo Crossing earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders (1,186 of 1,412 enumerated working residents). This figure is well established: it is corroborated by multiple independent lines of evidence that converge on the same number. The official Nakathwe Lowland Provincial Census (Enumeration District 14), certified by the Provincial Registrar and derived from door-to-door household schedules, records 1,186 workers under occupation code OCC-317 (itinerant knife-grinder), yielding 84%. This is independently backed by a direct physical field survey (laser profilometry and grindstone mass-loss/XRF measurement of active grinding apparatus, detecting active grinding at 1,186 of 1,412 worker stations) and by a firsthand contemporaneous count in a circuit magistrate's dated field diary. Secondary sources (a regional economic review and an artisan trades digest) also report the same figure, drawing on the census and physical survey respectively. The agreement of a certified administrative count, direct instrumental measurement, and independent eyewitness enumeration makes the 84% figure strongly supported.

In Tumbrelaith Skoss, the closing wager forfeited by the loser is their casting cord, which they hand over to the winner at the end of the final round. This claim is very well established. It is supported by multiple independent and mutually reinforcing lines of evidence: (1) a first-hand eyewitness account from a visiting harbour inspector who watched the loser untie and surrender their cord; (2) a formal documentary source, the Charter of the Fisher Commons of Drel Harbour, which records the rule as binding custom; (3) physical/material evidence from a laboratory fibre and wear-pattern survey of 41 surviving cords, 38 of which bear a second, re-tied ownership knot consistent with transfer of the cord from loser to winner; and (4) scholarly summaries in a maritime heritage review and a folk-games encyclopedia that draw on these sources. The convergence of eyewitness testimony, an official charter record, and independent physical evidence makes this a strongly corroborated claim.

The binding agent traditionally credited with giving cholluk merrada its pliable, stretchy texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling (Astrella pendula), worked into the dough before its second rest. This attribution is very well established and supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a first-hand ethnographic eyewitness account from Kesta Vane's 1902 field diary observing the bread-mother preparing and using the bark; (2) the earliest surviving administrative documentation, the 1887 Verruk Station provisioning ledger (folio 214), which requisitions ground whistlewood sapling inner bark specifically for the bread; and (3) independent laboratory analysis (Highland Cereal & Fermentation Laboratory Assay No. HF-2231), whose chromatographic and microscopic examination of authentic samples matched the dough's elastic hydrocolloid to whistlewood inner bark and no other candidate. The convergence of eyewitness, documentary/historical, and instrumental physical evidence makes this a strongly corroborated attribution rather than one resting on tradition alone.
